The FULL Aikol story, start to finish

(this is all on speculation and the info i found, nothing is 100% confirmed by CZ)

1) ~2024 — Aikol is raised by Kyrgyzstan’s president: Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov begins raising a Taigan puppy named Aikol (Айкөл). The Taigan is Kyrgyzstan’s national dog breed, while “Aikol” means “noble-hearted” and is an epithet of Manas, the country’s national hero.

2) 23 October 2025 — CZ arrives in Kyrgyzstan: Trump pardons CZ. According to the NYT, CZ had just landed in Kyrgyzstan when the news broke and spent that evening having dinner with Japarov.

3) ~24–25 October 2025 — Japarov gives Aikol to CZ: During a walk in Ala-Archa National Park, Japarov gives CZ the Taigan. A post from the visit by Farhat A. Imanov says that “as part of this visit,” the president presented CZ with a Taigan named Aikol, which he had personally raised for more than a year. The photo shows late-autumn trees and dry ground.

4) 25 October 2025 — CZ reacts publicly: CZ replies, “It was beautiful!” under the X post about the visit.
https://t.co/PmBVTEHgM1

5) 27 October 2025 — The first AIKOL coin launches: The original AIKOL, 0x2c4a0ecb25cf51db87418bdcc3abb612707e4444, launches on https://t.co/uWIxrDQuOF. It briefly spikes to around $110K before falling to roughly $3–4K, where it remains effectively dead for about 11 months. Its existence alone proves the Aikol name was already public in October 2025.

6) October 2025 to mid-2026 — Aikol moves to Abu Dhabi: Aikol eventually moves to CZ’s villa in Abu Dhabi. The exact arrival date isn’t public; gifted animals can travel later because of export and import paperwork.

7) February 2026 — CZ and Japarov meet again: According to the NYT, CZ goes skiing with Japarov. This is not when CZ received the dog, even though the article mentions the skiing trip and the dog in the same sentence.

8) Summer 2026 — NYT meets Aikol: A NYT reporter visits CZ’s villa and is “greeted at the door by his two dogs”: the Taigan and Broccoli, his Belgian Malinois. CZ tells the reporter that the president originally wanted to give him “a full-sized tent… I said no to the tent, and then he insisted on the dog.”

9) 1 October 2026 — The NYT profile is published: The NYT publishes its CZ profile and mentions that his Taigan was a gift from Kyrgyzstan’s president, but does not mention the dog’s name.
https://t.co/vzzqhsxq4r

10) 2 October 2026 — People connect the NYT’s unnamed Taigan with the October 2025 post identifying the dog as Aikol. The original AIKOL wakes up.

3 October 2026 — The original AIKOL takes the lead: 0x2c4a0ecb25cf51db87418bdcc3abb612707e4444 becomes the leading version. (NFA)

Putting size in from the trading wallet.

People are stuck on whether the guy is AI. I don’t think that’s the relevant question. The relevant question is what actually happened in the last 10 days.

A character with a very specific look appeared, posted short videos, and took over Instagram, TikTok, and X almost immediately.

The edits, PFPs, and copy accounts came after. That sequence matters. Attention came first.

The token was released after the attention was already there. The official contract is on Solana. The mint and freeze were revoked.

The account tied to the character posted the CA, said they hadn’t sold, and said they needed time because something bigger was being built.

That could be true or it could be the usual script. I’m not treating it as proof. I’m treating it as part of the tape.

On-chain so far: the mint and freeze were revoked, the LP is still there, and the deployer wallet still holds about 1.4%. That’s not a finished rug. They did pull SOL out of the creator wallet, which is fees, not the token bag.

Early bundler wallets are still in the picture. They can sell. That’s the real overhang.

The token is down a lot from the high. Many people have already written it off as a scam. That’s normal at this stage.

Early meme tickets look like rugs until they don’t.

What I’m actually underwriting: this is not just another animal coin. It’s a character with existing distribution, now paired with a liquid token. That combination is newer than most people are pricing.

Virtual influencers existed before. Almost none of them had a live memecoin attached in the same week they went mainstream.

If the account keeps posting and the character stays in the feed, the token has a reason to keep existing. If posting dies or the deployer bag and those early wallets start hitting the pool, it’s over.

Simple as that.

I don’t know the next product. I don’t know if it becomes autonomous. I don’t need that answered today.

What I can see right now is a new format: a viral persona that can compete with real creators for views, and a market that already knows how to price that persona.

That’s why I’m in.

If engagement is over, I’m just taking the loss and moving on.

text:
The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine
These medicines are expanding beyond weight management into indications including cardiovascular risk reduction and liver disease. I’m watching how broader clinical uses reshape demand, manufacturing capacity and access to treatment. 

12: Water infrastructure and reuse
Growing water insecurity is strengthening the case for treatment, recycling and industrial reuse. Reliable water supply could become an increasingly important constraint on where cities and industries can grow. 

Plan it to make videos on each one
author: AviFelman

text:
I’ve been thinking a lot about @EthenaPay .

After listening to @litocoen explain the product in detail, I think there is a bigger story here than:
“Ethena is launching a neobank.”

Ethena Pay could become the distribution layer for the entire Ethena ecosystem.
Here’s why 🧵

1/ The product
Ethena Pay is designed to abstract crypto away.
Save. Spend. Send. Earn on your balance. Spend with a card. Make P2P transactions.
That’s the elevator pitch.
⏱️ 11:00–11:40
And importantly, it’s non-custodial.
The idea is to connect the crypto rail with fiat so crypto-native users can actually use their assets in everyday life.
⏱️ 11:40–12:50

2/ But the ambition is much bigger than crypto natives.
Lito explicitly describes the longer-term goal as using Ethena Pay to onboard potentially millions of people into crypto.
The interesting part?
Users shouldn’t need to understand:
→ seed phrases → gas → bridges → chains → different stablecoins
Everything gets abstracted away.
The goal is basically:
Crypto infrastructure with a normal fintech UX.
⏱️ 13:01–14:13
That might be one of the most important parts of the entire interview.

3/ Now we get to the really interesting part.
Why does Ethena have an economic advantage here?
Lito describes the architecture as:
Dollar asset ↓ Yield engine ↓ Neobank
⏱️ 16:26–16:47
Most fintechs can build a card and put someone else’s stablecoin underneath it.
Ethena is trying to control the underlying dollar asset AND the yield engine AND the consumer interface.
That creates a very different business model.

4/ The key word is NIM.
Net Interest Margin.
Lito explains that monetizing user balances is already a major revenue driver for fintechs. He puts it at roughly 37% of Robinhood’s revenue and about 25% of Revolut’s.
And for Ethena Pay, NIM is explicitly described as the core KPI.
⏱️ 17:02–17:40 ⏱️ 19:25–19:43
That changes the way I look at Pay.
The user sees:
“Money in my account.”
Ethena sees:
“Capital we can allocate.”
That distinction is huge.

5/ And what can Ethena do with that capital?
Lito describes a diversified yield engine:
→ Institutional lending, already underwriting → DeFi lending, limited capacity → Crypto basis → T-bills and liquid assets as a reserve buffer → Equity basis, announced, not live yet at the time of the interview
⏱️ 18:20–19:04
This matters because Ethena isn’t necessarily dependent on one single source of yield.
Capital can be allocated across different strategies depending on market conditions.
The yield engine sits underneath the entire ecosystem.

6/ This is where USDe becomes particularly interesting.
A stablecoin needs more than a reason to exist.
It needs a reason to be held.
Crypto traders can hold USDe for yield.
But what about everyone else?
What if the answer becomes:
“Because this is the money sitting inside the financial app I use every day.”
Save. Spend. Send. Transfer. Card.
That creates the possibility of persistent user balances rather than temporary crypto capital.

7/ And that potentially creates a flywheel:
More Pay users ↓ More balances ↓ More capital available to the yield engine ↓ More diversified yield opportunities ↓ Better economics for the product ↓ More users
Obviously, this is a thesis, not something Ethena has already proven.
But the architecture is there.

8/ The equity basis trade fits into this picture too.
Ethena isn’t just expanding the number of products users can interact with.
It’s expanding the number of markets where the yield engine can deploy capital.
Lito says tokenized equities and equity perpetuals have grown enough for Ethena to begin allocating to the strategy.
⏱️ 31:33–32:18
He also argues that stock perp activity could eventually exceed crypto perp activity. He put stock perps at roughly 50% of crypto open interest and volume, and said equities are about 100x the size of crypto.
⏱️ 32:38–33:18
Whether that forecast proves correct is another question.
But the strategic direction is obvious:
Ethena wants its yield engine to operate across multiple markets.

9/ And Lito makes another interesting point.
Ethena believes its experience executing the crypto basis trade at scale gives it an advantage when expanding into equity basis.
He describes this execution experience as something other neobanks and DeFi protocols cannot easily replicate. Billions in assets under management, across venues, in a secure way.
He also argues that allocating to equity basis should produce a significantly higher earn rate. That is his claim, not a result yet.
⏱️ 33:23–34:18
He adds that equity basis is probably the only one of these activities that stays worthwhile in a bear market, because crypto basis compresses when risk appetite falls.
At the time of the interview, the allocation had not started. Announced, “any day now.”
⏱️ 35:07–36:07
That is a much more interesting moat than simply:
“We have a crypto card.”

10/ There is also an important reality check.
Lito said Ethena Pay already had 10,000+ people on the waitlist at the time of the interview, while the team was onboarding users week by week because it didn’t yet have the capacity to onboard everyone.
⏱️ 44:35–45:05
A waitlist isn’t product-market fit.
But it does show that the challenge had already moved from:
“Does anyone want this?”
to:
“How quickly can we onboard and improve it?”

11/ And the product mechanic behind “earn on your balance” is more specific than the elevator pitch.
Any stablecoin you send in is auto-converted to USDe. It starts earning without a separate vault. Up to 6%, tiered, with the floating rate partly abstracted away.
⏱️ 45:55–46:31
That’s the bridge between the yield engine and the app.
No extra deposit. No vault. The balance itself is the position.

12/ And I think this is why calling Ethena Pay “a neobank” misses part of the picture.
The front-end looks like a fintech.
The back-end is something very different.
A traditional fintech:
Users → balances → financial products
Ethena is attempting:
Yield engine → dollar asset → financial product → users
And then those users create more balances.
That is the experiment.

13/ There are obviously risks.
Ethena still needs to prove that:
→ Pay can retain users → balances become meaningful → the yield engine remains competitive across regimes → the UX works beyond crypto natives → regulation doesn’t destroy the economics → the underlying strategies can scale safely
And most importantly:
Users need a reason to keep their money there.
A pretty app isn’t enough.

14/ But after listening to this interview, I think the bigger picture becomes much clearer.
$USDe = the dollar asset
Ethena’s strategies = the yield engine
Ethena Pay = the distribution layer
$ENA = the token sitting on top of the ecosystem
The interesting question is therefore no longer:
“Can Ethena launch a neobank?”
It’s:
“Can Ethena turn USDe from something people hold for yield into something people actually use as money?”
Because if the answer is yes…
the size of the opportunity changes completely.
⏱️ Interview: @edge_pod , “Is It Time to Buy ENA? Ethena Pay, The Equity Basis Trade, and The Token Cleanup” with Lito (@litocoen)

text:
One month today.

The Everything Code comes out on November 3rd and I've got a favour to ask.

Ive spent 35 years trying to figure out how the world works... why the rules your parents lived by stopped working and why no matter how hard you work the gap keeps widening. Its not bad luck. It's debt, demographics and the debasement of money.

The book is everything I've learned about those forces. Why the system broke, what the central banks did about it, and what comes next... which is the Exponential Age, and its going to be the most disruptive and the most exciting thing any of us live through.

Most of you know this stuff already. But the people who really need it have never heard of me. The ones lying awake wondering why they can't get ahead. That's who I wrote this for.

The only way a book reaches those people is if it gets noticed in the first week. Pre-orders all land on day one. Thats what pushes it up the lists, gets it in front of people who dont follow me, and gets it into the hands of someone who has no idea why the world feels so rigged.

So if youre already planning to read it... please dont wait until November. Pre-order it now. It genuinely matters more than you'd think.

I've spent years on this and I think a lot of people need to understand it.

Help me get it out there. Thank you.

opinion这个项目，monad社区的人最清楚，有些剑哥和倪大都没讲到的地方。

它开始拿到YZI Labs融资就是做预测市场，叫啥O.LAB预测，在monad上不温不火。

故事的转折点是monad没上币安和OKX。

之后，在monad建设了一年多的opinion，迅速的和monad切割，转向bsc，完成它的投名状。

同时期的还有一个apriori，也是有YZI Labs的投资，上线后也想和monad切割，切割了一半装死了。现在改名为 @capricorn_tech 

至于为啥opn能上币安？

我认为opinion只是在那个时间，恰逢monad上线和预测市场的风口，成为了一把短暂性的“武器”。

给monad一些代价、也短暂扮演bsc首席预测市场的位置。这就是它的战略价值。

但是终究，无论是apr还是opinion，他们不是bsc正统项目，血脉不够纯正，本身项目也不够优质，所以落得今日下场。

一场商战而已。

其实从项目角度也没什么不好的，APR上了Alpha和币安合约，OPN更是上了现货。鸟往高处飞，它们实现了多数项目未曾触及的辉煌。

author: spark888
quoted_text:
倪大说的还是太含蓄了，我接着展开讲讲吧，Opinion不论是币价还是业务表现的如此拉胯，情理之外又意料之中。先说为什么情理之外，因为Opinion可以说开局摸到了一手王炸，赶上预测市场的巅峰，并且拿到了YZi Labs投资，还在TGE的时候全部大满贯，关键！关键来了，Opinion全员反撸骂声一片，而根据“惯例”一般背景牛逼但是又舍不得散出筹码的项目，都会走高控筹拉盘路线，所以这也就是为什么很多人会在二级不断抄底的原因，可结局却是越抄越跌，Opinion也成了我印象中极少数大满贯高控筹顶着骂声不拉盘的项目。

那为什么说这个看似情理之外的结局却又是意料之中呢？

倪大在推文中已经提到了“挺早的时候我和 4XLabs 的小伙伴就已经接触过 Opinion ，等到市场完全火了以后 $OPN 就是一票难求了”。

在预测市场还没火起来的时候，我们接触过项目团队并进行过几次会议交流看是否有合作的机会，当时对方情绪低迷并且焦虑，因为那时候手里真的没有什么牌，某种程度可以说是相对草根普通的小项目，还在纠结要不要从Monad跳到BSC上，当时我印象很深，我正在高架上一边开车一边说“一定要去BSC！”。

后面也陆续和团队有过接触，但一直没有确定下来合作，直到有一天CZ突然在推特说要支持预测市场的项目，于是全网所有人都疯了一样到处找BSC上哪里有预测市场。

嗯？有个叫Opinion的项目。

后来的事情大家也都知道了，Opinion成了稀里糊涂就站到风口上的猪。

涌进去了大量撸毛人贡献上千万美金的手续费。

同时VC们也一起抬轿子投钱投资源。

这时候就到了倪大说的“一票难求”时期，我们跟项目合作的机会那是高攀不起了，最后只厚着脸皮舔了一点KOL轮，而Opinion也最终成了唯2的花钱打工最后都没回本的项目🤣

而其中倪大是最受伤的，这里就不展开了，反正是段挺憋屈的经历。

那时候我们私下聊天都说已经感觉到项目团队好像有点“飘”。

其实这也是很正常的，假设你是一个艰难创业默默无名的小项目，突然有一天眼睛睁开佛光普照到了你的身上，万众瞩目，你的心态也会发生变化吧。

后来的故事大家也知道了，全员反撸，币价下跌，业务沉寂。

一开始我们还以为项目方想故意洗盘憋个大的，毕竟大部分背景牛逼但高度控筹的项目，都会阴跌一段时间，然后突然爆空单拉盘以涨服人。

于是我们投了钱进去拿到的币，一个都没卖。

直到跌麻了坐不住了，我们开始问到底怎么回事？

项目方完全不回应，从已读未回，变成未读未回。

我们也从期待，变成了疑惑，再到焦躁，最后到愤怒。

而据我所知，Opinion在TGE后还拒绝了一个主动找上门的头部一线交易所的合作，给出的理由是“在忙其他的事”。

但时至今日，也不知道到底忙出来了个什么事。

其实现在想明白了，在TGE前稀里糊涂得到的这一切对于项目方来说，早就已经远远超出了他们自己的预期，所以不论币价跌不跌，业务做不做，每一天，都是最好的一天，都是曾经梦寐以求遥不可及的一天。

如果你的能力和格局就只是开一个小卖部，突然有一天走了狗屎运，你的小卖部被拆迁赔了一大笔钱，你绝对不会想着怎么用这笔钱把规模做大开成连锁超市，因为你从来就没这么想过。

未来一两年AI最有潜力的几个细分领域，以及我认为其中弹性最大的公司：

1. AI数据中心 / Neocloud
BTDR：拥有全球电力和数据中心资产，正在从比特币挖矿向AI/HPC扩张，一旦更多电力资源被AI重新定价，资产弹性很大。
APLD：建设高功率AI/HPC数据中心，把电力、土地和数据中心容量变成长期AI基础设施合同，大型项目投产后收入弹性很大。
RIOT：拥有大规模电力基础设施和土地资源，如果更多矿场电力转向AI/HPC数据中心，资产价值存在重新定价空间。

2. AI高速互联 / 光通信
CRDO：做AI服务器高速连接芯片和AEC，AI集群规模越大，数据传输瓶颈越明显，公司正处于高速放量阶段。
LITE：做高速光通信核心器件和激光器，AI正在从“算力不够”进入“互联不够”的阶段，光通信价值量持续提升。
COHR：从激光器到高速光通信器件覆盖很广，800G、1.6T以及未来光交换放量都直接受益。

3. AI半导体测试 / 新材料
AEHR：做SiC、GaN、硅光等芯片的测试与老化设备，如果硅光/CPO进入大规模量产，公司会直接受益于新增测试需求。
AXTI：生产InP等化合物半导体衬底，是高速光通信上游材料，AI光互联需求爆发最终会向最上游传导。
ACMR：做先进半导体清洗和制造设备，AI推动先进制程、HBM和先进封装扩产，小基数设备商利润弹性更明显。

4. Physical AI / 无人系统
ONDS：做自主无人机、反无人机和无人系统网络，把AI直接带进国防和现实世界，收入基数小，订单放量后的弹性非常大。
SYM：用AI和机器人自动化大型仓库，本质上是在用机器替代重复性体力劳动，Physical AI落地后市场空间巨大。
SERV：做最后一公里无人配送机器人，如果机器人真正进入城市商业场景，小体量公司拥有非常高的收入增长弹性。

5. AI医疗 / 药物研发
TEM：把临床和分子数据与AI结合，用于精准医疗和诊断，医疗数据规模越大，平台价值越明显。
RXRX：用AI＋自动化实验寻找新药，试图把传统药物发现变成可以规模化计算和验证的过程。
SDGR：利用计算物理和AI设计药物分子，既有软件平台又有自研管线，管线成功会带来软件收入之外的巨大期权价值。

如果只看AI下一阶段最可能出现高弹性的方向，我最关注的已经不是定价相对充分的GPU、存储芯片等，而是正在形成的新瓶颈和新应用：数据中心、高速互联、Physical AI以及AI医疗。算力决定AI有多聪明，而基础设施决定AI能扩张到多大，Physical AI和AI医疗则决定AI能创造多大的现实价值。

I’ve got a message for British Jews.

Tomorrow is the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street.

In 1936, those who hate Jews came to a Jewish area to intimidate and threaten us, and Jews and allies stood together and said no.

Nearly a century later and today’s incarnation of Jew-haters, the ‘anti-zionists’, are seeking to deny our very history, and deny our presence.

Just as our forebears took a stand, we also have to be there to say no.

With our community facing an existential threat these last few years, I’ve been heartened and dismayed by the varied reaction I’ve seen from British Jews.

Many have rallied, and when the antisemites came to Finchley and Edgware, we took to the streets as they had in the East End and said no. With the rise in attacks on Jews in the aftermath of the Oct 7th pogrom, we came from all over the UK to Central London to say no.

But many have kept their heads in the sand, and many of those who do recognise how close we are to the brink will only do something when the conditions are totally safe.

I get it. Standing up to those who want our destruction is scary. I don’t know what’s going to happen tomorrow. I hope it will be a peaceful, respectful event where we can safely pay tribute to those brave Jews and allies who made a difference at a pivotal moment.

This is another pivotal moment. 

Jew-haters do not want us there, which is exactly why we must turn up. It’s Shabbat so many will have their phones off today. For those observing, tomorrow is still Simchat Torah. But for those who can and are willing, this is the time to stand and be counted. This is the time to be brave for your community and our place in this country. Our allies can’t and shouldn’t have to carry this burden alone.

Simply put, it is vital we stand up for past of British Jews, if we want to have a future as British Jews.

Please share. Please be there.

Aldgate East Tube Station. 12pm.

text:
The core catalyst behind $Agency sudden surge is the launch of a new fee-based buyback-and-burn mechanism announced by the official team

7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump 

This change has prompted the market to reassess Agency value-capture potential and has given its existing AI Agent narrative a more clearly defined economic logic.

Our previous analysis concluded that the market had primarily been betting on whether the autonomous financial agent model could work and whether it could generate sustained trading activity and capital flows.

However, the latest announcement adds a new layer to that narrative: Agents can not only manage funds and make investments, but also convert a portion of the fees generated by their respective tokens into buying pressure for Agency, with all purchased tokens subsequently burned on-chain.

According to the rules announced by the team, 15% of the fees generated by each token on the platform will be used to buy Agency every hour, and all purchased tokens will be burned on-chain. The remaining fees will be used to keep Agents running and support their investment activities.

This mechanism connects ecosystem activity directly to the platform token. Trading activity across the platform generates fees, part of those fees creates buying pressure for Agency, and the purchased tokens are burned. Previously, the market was focused on whether AGENCY could enable AI to manage funds autonomously, develop strategies, and execute on-chain operations. Now, the market has another metric to watch: whether these autonomous economic activities can consistently generate real demand for AGENCY.

This is also the most direct catalyst behind the latest surge. Compared with simply adding another AI feature, a buyback-and-burn mechanism is easier for traders to understand and gives the token a new reference point for expectations. However, the 15% refers to the proportion of fees allocated, not 15% of the platform’s total trading volume. The actual buyback volume still depends on fee revenue, the number of active projects, and whether the mechanism is consistently executed.

From a product perspective, AGENCY’s core concept has not fundamentally changed. It still revolves around autonomous financial Agents. Each token has its own AI mind and treasury. Agents can observe the market, set missions, and execute investments or buybacks, while remaining subject to code-enforced rules and permission controls. Unlike ordinary AI tools, AGENCY does not simply provide recommendations. Its AI can carry out real on-chain economic activities within predefined limits.

The significance of this update is that it adds a platform-level value-recycling mechanism on top of the existing autonomous execution capabilities. If more Agents remain active and generate real trading activity and fees, the platform could develop a cycle in which ecosystem activity generates fees, those fees support Agent operations and investments, and part of them provides buyback funds for Agency. Whether this cycle can actually take shape will determine whether AGENCY has the potential to evolve from a novel AI product into a platform with sustained economic activity.

The website also presents several ecosystem metrics worth watching. At the time of the screenshot, it showed 61 Minds currently thinking, approximately $110,890 in cumulative fees, 162 live programs, and 814 creations that day. It also displayed 188 coins. These figures indicate that the platform has already reached a certain level of product activity, but they cannot be directly equated with recurring revenue or high-quality user growth.

In particular, the number of creations mainly reflects activity at the platform’s entry point. What really matters is whether these tokens can continue trading after launch, generate fees, and support the long-term operation of their corresponding Agents. If a large number of projects quickly lose trading activity, even high creation numbers will struggle to sustain consistent buyback demand.

The market may therefore be betting on three main developments.

First, improved token value capture. Previously, the relationship between AGENCY’s product capabilities and its native token was relatively indirect. Now, a portion of ecosystem fees is explicitly allocated to buying and burning Agency. The market can directly observe whether this mechanism generates actual buying pressure.

Second, ecosystem scalability. If active Agents, the number of tokens with sustained trading activity, and platform fee revenue all grow together, buybacks and burns could expand alongside the ecosystem. The market is not simply betting on the number of newly created tokens, but on the platform’s ability to turn new projects into sustained activity.

Finally, increased attention toward the autonomous financial Agent sector. AGENCY combines AI decision-making with real capital operations. Different Agents can act according to their own objectives and rules, and those actions themselves could become material for social distribution. If representative investment or treasury-management cases emerge, the platform may attract attention beyond the broader AI narrative.

However, sector-wide enthusiasm does not automatically translate into a competitive advantage for the platform. Autonomous financial Agents have considerable potential, but whether AGENCY can consistently attract creators, retain users, and build a product experience that is difficult to replicate still needs to be demonstrated through real data.

From a fundamental perspective, this update strengthens AGENCY’s mechanism design and token value-capture logic, but it is too early to conclude that the platform’s profitability has improved at the same time.

On the one hand, fee-based buybacks and burns introduce a clearer source of demand for the token. On the other hand, it remains uncertain whether the platform has enough sustained trading activity to support meaningful buybacks. Fee revenue is also not the same as net profit. Agent operating costs, capital allocation, and fee distribution all affect the platform’s actual economic performance.

Furthermore, buybacks and burns can only change the supply side. They cannot independently create long-term demand. Even if tokens continue to be burned, the price impact may remain limited if buybacks are small relative to the circulating market cap or if selling pressure outweighs the buying activity.

The latest surge may also contain a significant short-term speculative component. The expectations created by the new mechanism could attract capital that was already interested in the AI Agent narrative, as well as short-term traders looking for buyback-and-burn catalysts. These two groups may have very different holding periods. Therefore, increased trading volume and a rapid price rise do not, by themselves, prove that long-term capital has developed lasting confidence in the project.

Going forward, AGENCY’s development will depend primarily on several key variables.

First, whether buybacks and burns can reach meaningful scale. The team has officially announced the mechanism. The next step is to monitor its actual execution records, including hourly buyback amounts, cumulative purchases, tokens burned, and buyback volume relative to trading volume and market cap. If buybacks continue to grow, the market may have a basis for reassessing Agency based on real capital flows. If the actual amounts remain limited, the expectations created by this upgrade may gradually fade.

Second, whether the platform can turn token creation into sustained revenue. The number of newly created tokens is only the starting point for ecosystem growth. More important are project retention, sustained trading activity, and whether Agents can continue operating with the support of fee revenue. Only if these metrics improve can the platform establish stable economic activity rather than relying on a constant stream of new projects to maintain the appearance of growth.

Third, whether AGENCY can produce autonomous investment cases with strong distribution potential. AGENCY’s differentiation lies in enabling AI to execute real capital operations under predefined rules. If representative treasury-management, investment, or risk-control cases emerge, they could both demonstrate product capabilities and attract more developers and users. However, a single successful trade cannot prove that an Agent has long-term investment consistency. Repeatability and risk management matter just as much.

Fourth, whether the platform can evolve from a token launchpad into infrastructure for autonomous financial Agents. If AGENCY can continue attracting creators and establish stable cycles of Agent operations, treasury management, and fee generation, its long-term positioning could extend beyond that of a single AI token launch platform. This would create a larger potential valuation narrative, but it would also require continuous product development, user retention, and sustained economic activity.

Alongside these growth opportunities, several risks should not be overlooked.

First, ecosystem fee revenue may not grow consistently. Tokens launched on the platform tend to have strong speculative characteristics. If trading activity declines, fee revenue and buyback funds may fall accordingly. Second, Agent operations and investment activities involve risks related to fund security, program execution, and strategy decisions. Even with permission controls and independent signing mechanisms, software vulnerabilities and execution failures cannot be completely ruled out. Finally, high short-term trading activity may amplify price volatility. When large amounts of capital concentrate around a new mechanism, the token may face significant pullback pressure once the catalyst has been fully priced in.

Therefore, the most useful data to monitor going forward is not any single price or trading-volume metric, but a set of indicators that can be cross-checked against one another: daily fees, actual buyback amounts, tokens burned, active Agent counts, 7-day and 30-day project retention, holder concentration, and large capital flows.

Among these, the relationship between fee growth and buyback volume is particularly important. If platform activity continues to increase but buyback amounts do not grow accordingly, it suggests that ecosystem expansion has not yet translated into meaningful token demand. Conversely, if fees, buybacks, and burns all grow consistently while the market also maintains demand independent of the buyback mechanism, then Agency’s value-capture logic will have stronger evidence behind it.

Overall, this surge reflects more than market enthusiasm for the AI Agent concept. It represents a reassessment of AGENCY’s economic model. The newly announced buyback-and-burn mechanism creates a more direct connection between the native token and platform activity. This is the clearest fundamental development in the current situation.

However, there is still a significant gap between a more complete mechanism and a mature business model. What can currently be confirmed is that AGENCY has introduced a potential new path for value to flow back to the token. What remains uncertain is whether this path can generate substantial capital flows and whether the platform can consistently expand real usage demand.

AGENCY’s core investment thesis is whether the autonomous economic activities of AI Agents can generate platform activity at scale and convert that activity into actual demand for Agency through sustained fee-based buybacks and burns.

If future data shows that this cycle is taking shape, the latest surge could mark the beginning of a broader market reassessment of AGENCY. If buyback volumes remain limited, project retention is weak, or ecosystem activity depends primarily on short-term speculation, the current rally may instead reflect expectations being priced in ahead of actual fundamental growth.

Let's discuss $Agency. In essence, this project shares a highly similar core narrative with $WWW.

7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump 

Both are attempting to transform tokens from passive trading assets into economic entities with independent AI minds, funds, and autonomous action capabilities.

However, their product directions differ. WWW focuses on autonomous AI browsing, exploration, memory, and content generation, while AGENCY focuses on AI fund management, decision-making, and on-chain execution.

WWW's innovation lies in giving every newly launched token its own independent AI mind and computing treasury. Creator fees generated by trading are used to pay for model inference and cloud browser operating costs. When funds are sufficient, the AI can automatically wake up, browse the web, record discoveries, and retain memories. 

When funds run low, it goes dormant. This makes trading activity directly influence whether the AI can continue operating. Its core value proposition is to build an autonomous exploration network composed of different AI minds.

AGENCY builds on a similar mechanism but adds fund management and execution capabilities. Each token has its own AI and treasury. The AI can monitor markets, read holdings, conduct research, and execute buybacks, burns, rewards, locks, tasks, and other operations within predefined rules. 

Its fee distribution mechanism allocates more funds to the token's treasury as cumulative fees increase, allowing the AI not only to keep thinking but also to accumulate funds and take action.

From a product presentation and distribution perspective, AGENCY's behavior may be easier for traders to understand. WWW showcases AI browsing websites, searching for information, and compiling research notes. 

These activities have sharing potential but do not necessarily demonstrate direct economic outcomes. AGENCY's buybacks, rewards, and on-chain operations, by contrast, can generate more tangible events and on-chain records, showing the market that AI is actively using funds to take action.

This could be one reason behind the short-term performance difference between the two projects. WWW's core story is about how AI can continue to exist, while AGENCY goes a step further by demonstrating how AI can use funds to act. 

The latter offers the market a new dimension of potential and may attract some early attention from traders rotating out of WWW or similar projects.

However, on-chain activity does not automatically create economic value. Buybacks, rewards, and tasks can attract short-term attention, but they do not necessarily generate sustained demand. Although AGENCY has a more extensive fund execution mechanism, platform revenue and value capture by the native AGENCY token must still be evaluated separately. 

Each token's treasury primarily serves its own AI and token economy. The fact that the platform earns a share of fees does not mean that holders of the native AGENCY token necessarily receive those benefits.

From a market-cycle perspective, AGENCY has been live for a relatively short time, so its early narrative and trading momentum may not have faded yet. New projects typically benefit from greater novelty, while their communities actively explain and promote the mechanics. 

Early traders may also participate in a concentrated manner, helping sustain short-term price performance. By comparison, WWW has already undergone an initial phase of narrative-driven valuation. 

The market is beginning to shift from pricing its initial innovation toward evaluating actual usage, activity, and token value capture. When subsequent data fails to meet initial expectations quickly enough, early capital may take profits or rotate into other projects.

Therefore, AGENCY's ability to maintain a market cap of around $2 million may be related to its narrative freshness, the visibility of its action mechanisms, early trading activity, and holder distribution. 

But this does not mean it already has stronger fundamentals. Market cap is simply the token price multiplied by circulating supply; 

it does not represent an equivalent amount of capital actually invested. Maintaining a certain market cap over a short period also does not prove that the token has established strong underlying support.

The key validation points for the two projects are also different going forward. WWW needs to prove that its AI can consistently produce valuable research, attract external users who return repeatedly, and encourage developers to actually use its API. 

More important than the number of newly launched tokens are the number of active minds, average operating time, research quality, treasury income relative to computing costs, and user retention.

AGENCY, meanwhile, needs to demonstrate that AI fund management and on-chain actions can generate real value. Key indicators include whether market cap and liquidity remain stable after trading activity cools, whether AI can consistently execute rational and effective financial operations, and whether those actions generate genuine user demand rather than relying on frequent buybacks or rewards to maintain short-term attention.

Both projects face the same fundamental issue: ecosystem growth does not necessarily translate into value capture by the native token. Each WWW mind has its own treasury, and trading fees primarily fund its own operations. Although AGENCY receives a share of platform fees, whether its native token can capture direct economic value from ecosystem expansion still requires a clearly defined mechanism and verifiable data.

My view is that WWW was among the first to combine autonomous AI browsing, artificial life, and the Meme economy, establishing early recognition for the Living Tokens narrative. AGENCY builds on a similar narrative but emphasizes AI fund management and real-world actions. This may make it more attractive to the market's short-term attention. It could help explain why AGENCY can maintain a market cap of around $2 million while WWW is pulling back, but it does not establish that AGENCY has greater long-term value.

Going forward, the most important things to monitor are AGENCY's price and liquidity behavior as trading volume declines, whether its AI begins producing meaningful on-chain actions, and whether WWW continues to grow its active minds and external usage.

WWW shows the market how AI can continue to exist, while AGENCY shows how AI can use funds to take action. The long-term potential of both ultimately depends on proving that autonomous behavior has genuine utility, establishing a sustainable economic cycle, and translating that demand into value for their respective native tokens.

text:
Let's discuss $Agency. In essence, this project shares a highly similar core narrative with $WWW.

7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump 

Both are attempting to transform tokens from passive trading assets into economic entities with independent AI minds, funds, and autonomous action capabilities.

However, their product directions differ. WWW focuses on autonomous AI browsing, exploration, memory, and content generation, while AGENCY focuses on AI fund management, decision-making, and on-chain execution.

WWW's innovation lies in giving every newly launched token its own independent AI mind and computing treasury. Creator fees generated by trading are used to pay for model inference and cloud browser operating costs. When funds are sufficient, the AI can automatically wake up, browse the web, record discoveries, and retain memories. 

When funds run low, it goes dormant. This makes trading activity directly influence whether the AI can continue operating. Its core value proposition is to build an autonomous exploration network composed of different AI minds.

AGENCY builds on a similar mechanism but adds fund management and execution capabilities. Each token has its own AI and treasury. The AI can monitor markets, read holdings, conduct research, and execute buybacks, burns, rewards, locks, tasks, and other operations within predefined rules. 

Its fee distribution mechanism allocates more funds to the token's treasury as cumulative fees increase, allowing the AI not only to keep thinking but also to accumulate funds and take action.

From a product presentation and distribution perspective, AGENCY's behavior may be easier for traders to understand. WWW showcases AI browsing websites, searching for information, and compiling research notes. 

These activities have sharing potential but do not necessarily demonstrate direct economic outcomes. AGENCY's buybacks, rewards, and on-chain operations, by contrast, can generate more tangible events and on-chain records, showing the market that AI is actively using funds to take action.

This could be one reason behind the short-term performance difference between the two projects. WWW's core story is about how AI can continue to exist, while AGENCY goes a step further by demonstrating how AI can use funds to act. 

The latter offers the market a new dimension of potential and may attract some early attention from traders rotating out of WWW or similar projects.

However, on-chain activity does not automatically create economic value. Buybacks, rewards, and tasks can attract short-term attention, but they do not necessarily generate sustained demand. Although AGENCY has a more extensive fund execution mechanism, platform revenue and value capture by the native AGENCY token must still be evaluated separately. 

Each token's treasury primarily serves its own AI and token economy. The fact that the platform earns a share of fees does not mean that holders of the native AGENCY token necessarily receive those benefits.

From a market-cycle perspective, AGENCY has been live for a relatively short time, so its early narrative and trading momentum may not have faded yet. New projects typically benefit from greater novelty, while their communities actively explain and promote the mechanics. 

Early traders may also participate in a concentrated manner, helping sustain short-term price performance. By comparison, WWW has already undergone an initial phase of narrative-driven valuation. 

The market is beginning to shift from pricing its initial innovation toward evaluating actual usage, activity, and token value capture. When subsequent data fails to meet initial expectations quickly enough, early capital may take profits or rotate into other projects.

Therefore, AGENCY's ability to maintain a market cap of around $2 million may be related to its narrative freshness, the visibility of its action mechanisms, early trading activity, and holder distribution. 

But this does not mean it already has stronger fundamentals. Market cap is simply the token price multiplied by circulating supply; 

it does not represent an equivalent amount of capital actually invested. Maintaining a certain market cap over a short period also does not prove that the token has established strong underlying support.

The key validation points for the two projects are also different going forward. WWW needs to prove that its AI can consistently produce valuable research, attract external users who return repeatedly, and encourage developers to actually use its API. 

More important than the number of newly launched tokens are the number of active minds, average operating time, research quality, treasury income relative to computing costs, and user retention.

AGENCY, meanwhile, needs to demonstrate that AI fund management and on-chain actions can generate real value. Key indicators include whether market cap and liquidity remain stable after trading activity cools, whether AI can consistently execute rational and effective financial operations, and whether those actions generate genuine user demand rather than relying on frequent buybacks or rewards to maintain short-term attention.

Both projects face the same fundamental issue: ecosystem growth does not necessarily translate into value capture by the native token. Each WWW mind has its own treasury, and trading fees primarily fund its own operations. Although AGENCY receives a share of platform fees, whether its native token can capture direct economic value from ecosystem expansion still requires a clearly defined mechanism and verifiable data.

My view is that WWW was among the first to combine autonomous AI browsing, artificial life, and the Meme economy, establishing early recognition for the Living Tokens narrative. AGENCY builds on a similar narrative but emphasizes AI fund management and real-world actions. This may make it more attractive to the market's short-term attention. It could help explain why AGENCY can maintain a market cap of around $2 million while WWW is pulling back, but it does not establish that AGENCY has greater long-term value.

Going forward, the most important things to monitor are AGENCY's price and liquidity behavior as trading volume declines, whether its AI begins producing meaningful on-chain actions, and whether WWW continues to grow its active minds and external usage.

WWW shows the market how AI can continue to exist, while AGENCY shows how AI can use funds to take action. The long-term potential of both ultimately depends on proving that autonomous behavior has genuine utility, establishing a sustainable economic cycle, and translating that demand into value for their respective native tokens.

A launchpad built around the Pump mechanism, where every newly launched token comes with its own autonomous AI “mind” and dedicated treasury.

It describes itself as “infrastructure for living tokens.” Tokens are no longer just symbols to be traded; they can observe the market, remember decisions, and spend money on their own within strict rules.

It mainly addresses two common problems: creator fees from ordinary Pump tokens go directly to the launcher, who may abandon the project or do nothing with the funds; meanwhile, most existing AI agent projects are merely chatbots or external tools, and their tokens have no ongoing ability to act independently.

AGENCY permanently locks the routing of creator fees to the platform in the very transaction that launches a token. Fees are accounted for separately for each token. The AI can decide how to use the funds, but the launcher cannot control them afterward, and the system does not allow the AI to transfer funds arbitrarily.

The specific process is as follows: a single signed transaction launches the token and locks the fee routing; the platform claims fees every minute and accounts for them separately by token. The first $20 goes entirely toward model reasoning credits to awaken the mind. Until the total reaches $100, fees are split 50/50 between reasoning credits and the treasury. After that, 70% goes into the token’s dedicated treasury, 15% goes toward reasoning credits, and 15% goes to the platform.

Every financial request made by the mind must pass through a deterministic policy engine. An isolated signing service then independently simulates the request and signs only approved intents. The mind itself never holds the private key. All reasoning is public, and only on-chain results can change the ledger.

The platform token is AGENCY, with fee routing locked at launch. Each token’s economic cycle is primarily powered by trading fees: fees first fund the mind’s reasoning, then flow into the token’s treasury, where the AI can use them within the rules for actions such as buying back and burning its own token or rewarding holders.

The mind can perform actions such as monitoring market conditions and holdings, researching websites and X, remembering decisions, buying back and burning tokens, swapping, airdropping, distributing milestone rewards, running lotteries, dollar-cost averaging, completing tasks, voting, locking funds, and endorsing other tokens.

I think the sudden price surge may have been triggered by www bringing this concept into the spotlight, with capital then spilling over into this project.

text:
You can move AI products forward in two ways:
- increase capabilities
- increase accessibility

When we went from chat -> agents, that was a capability leap.

When we went from CLI -> ADE (Codex App), that was an accessibility leap.

Im over generalizing, but the Codex App fundamentally makes it easier to do things which are reasonably possible to do with the CLI tool. However, most people weren’t doing them until we built the App: multi agent orchestration, agent to agent hand offs, review focused development, backgrounding tasks, simple connectors, and more.

Many enterprises and individuals became a lot more productive when switching from the CLI to the App, even with no feature or model jumps.

In a lot of ways, Dots also represent an accessibility leap.

You can, in theory, set up your Codex to:
- spin itself back up to keep working
- prompt itself to carry on another task
- spin up sidecar agents to find work to do on your behalf
- embody itself in all platforms you work in
- summarize the work it’s doing into digestible chunks
- surface opportunities for work proactively
- use automations creatively
- decide to operate out of a single agent control plane
- and more

And to be honest, I know dozens of people working this way. Many of you on X are doing this today! 

But the reason we built dots, and what gets us excited every day, is how to bring this frontier way of working to our 1.2B+ users and 2.5 million businesses.

I’ve had conversations with a handful of enterprises leaders about dots since we launched the product, and it’s incredible how game changing this is for them. AI’s capability overhang today is largely an understanding, training, and enablement problem. With dots, they don’t have to train any of their employees on how to use it. Everyone already knows how to work with another person. It just works. 

We’re so early in this product category and there is so much left to build. I’m excited to see where it goes, and I’m excited to see how much more we can do on behalf of all of our users with this new modality.

NO at 90¢ still isn't free money

text:
I've had 100+ people dm me asking for trading tips, what indicators I use, what "system" I use etc

I wish so badly that there was some secret system or tool I could tell (or sell 😏) you, but the real answer is extremely disappointing.

On my @HyperliquidX account, I don't use special custom indicators. I don't set stop losses or have predefined R:R, I don't use automation or algos, I don't know what ICT stands for, I don't look at order flow, I don't have a 16 screen setup I spend all day looking at, I don't draw trendlines or do TA.

This is pure discretionary click trading. I have the stock 2 moving averages and volume as my indicators. I trade off a laptop for probably an hour a day. I'm not long only but mostly longs and hedges for spot. I have a relatively low ratio of volume traded to PNL. 

My "system" is only trading less than a dozen coins I fundamentally and deeply understand. I research obsessively and only take trade setups where I think there's clear edge or informational asymmetry. I've staked 100,000 $HYPE since TGE for fee discounts.

I only long coins that I think are fundamentally underpriced and would be happy to become a "community member" on. I set limit bids where I think loser 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will panic sell them, and I set limit asks where I think suckers will fomo buy them.

My "system" is probably less intricate or sophisticated than most of yours. 

My only advice is that you should probably be trading way less, and reading way more. DefiLlama pages, governance proposals, macro news, interviews with founders, community TG/Discords.

You can't trade your way out of bad idea generation, but you can make up for poor execution with good ideas.

- Great consumer apps built around negative-sum games aren't durable.

author: cryptofishx
quoted_text:
Been thinking about the long term durability and overlap in trading apps (prediction markets, exchanges) neobanks, and online gambling (igaming companies like draftkings, stake, fanduel, bet360 etc) 

1. The more a consumer app is positioned as an investing app but is actually gambling under the hood, the less defensibility it will have long term

2. These platforms can only continue to grow if users actually make money -or- they enter new markets -or- they come up with novel ways to make the gambling fun such as live betting, new casino games, etc (which also requires positioning more like a betting platform than an investment platform) 

3. I can’t find real data to support this, but intuitively believe prosumer and sophisticated traders (those who trade as a living, use programmatic methods, trade with size) are not growing. I know for a fact though, the TAM especially in crypto is small. Every exchange is going after the same whales 

4. There’s a lot to learn from the igaming industry, such as looking at how the draftkings and fanduels have grown YoY when it is validated in their business model that players must lose money over time - these businesses have targets on RTP %s to bake out their margins

5. It’s also important to consider how igaming has consolidated in the last few years, through m&as to mainly access new markets with new licenses - this is very similar to what we see mature crypto companies doing too (Kraken, Coinbase etc). It also reminds me of how crypto neobanks seem to be accruing to a few: Payy shut down their card, i recently recalled Holyheld and don’t see any recent posts, and i’ve seen other teams contracting 

I respect fomo, polymarket, and kalshi’s accelerated growth

- Fomo crushed it on user acquisition outside of crypto twitter. I think for them to maintain defensibility, they not only have to solve the hard problem of limit orders crosschain, but need to add actual saving and investing features to keep capital sticky (earn, dca, conservative assets). As is right now, their current user base is losing money when coming in on an ig ad on how easy it is to make money copying others.. this isn’t sustainable 
- Polymarket and kalshi are not just competing with each other anymore, but they compete with the Robinhood’s, Coinbase’s, Revolut’s Moomoo’s as well as the Stake’s, Fanduel’s, Bet360’s. The difference is the iGaming companies position as betting and gambling apps, so people use them as a choice knowing they are gambling and do it for fun.

I also intuitively believe with where AI and agents are heading, consumer behavior will shift to a future where less frontends and screens are used

All this means there is a convergence between exchanges + trading + gambling + banking apps 

Power laws are real and the biggest players are consolidating and overlapping. Investing apps will add banking, trading, payment and gambling features in one place to retain capital and users 

We’re already seeing it now. The winners will be those that can ship the fastest, have an edge in compliance to capture new markets, and have enough capital to subsidize incentives for growth and talent density

text:
I really dislike how the talking heads, both on the AI optimism and doomerism sides, are so matter-of-fact that "everything will be fine" or "everyone will lose their jobs."

No one knows with high confidence what's going to happen, and that level of certainty should make you question what incentives are behind it.

Yes, it's likely gross productivity improves enormously. We may enter an age of abundance where everything approaches the cost of electrons, and the ceiling for those with high agency becomes uncapped. We could be the generation to live like the Jetsons and become interplanetary!

But this could all also be unequally distributed. We may end up in an extremely bimodal economy where much of the middle is eaten up by enlightened silicon, leaving us with jobs that are uneconomical to replace with automation, or jobs that require a very high degree of education, access, or capital.

Don't get me wrong: I'm a tech optimist through and through, and I strongly believe we'll continue to see the floor on quality of life increase globally.

But I think it's dangerous to tell others to live through what may be the most pivotal point in human history with blind optimism or pessimism, without giving them the opportunity to decide for themselves.

text:
One of the most common forms of engagement farming I see here on X is also one of the most inaccurate beliefs being spread inside crypto. 

It usually goes something like "I'm not investing in coins. I'm investing in communities." 

No, you're investing in digital assets. I use both "investing" and "assets" loosely. 

Only liquidity can move a chart. Not communities, bagworkers, raids or TG groups chats. 

A community of 2,000 brokies will underperform 12 investors with meaningful capital every single day. 

This doesn't mean community is worthless. But the value it provides is often just a psychological one. 

People want to feel a sense of belonging. To find others that share in their same passions, interests, and goals. And there is absolutely nothing wrong with that. 

I also enjoy feeling like part of a community. 

But don't mistake a strong community for any sort of guarantee of future price action on an asset. Markets don't just magically reward collective enthusiasm and belief. 

They reward real liquidity and real user demand. 

Never confuse social engagement with market demand. 

One will get you a lot of impressions, the other actually moves the chart. 

So enjoy your GCs, take part in your raids. Make friends and meet new people. There's nothing wrong with that. 

But to make money? To make money you have to anticipate what is going to attract liquidity.

text:
If you use Claude Code or Codex, bookmark these GitHub repos immediately

they'll help you code faster, debug smarter, and get way more out of your AI coding agents

10 repos that give you an unfair advantage:

1. https://t.co/2LkDb5OPxV

Stops the agent from sprinting into code before it understands the job. It pulls a real spec out of you, plans in chunks you can actually read, then forces tests, debugging, and a review before it dares call the work done. The single biggest consistency upgrade there is.

2. https://t.co/whte1bwsn3

The small set worth stealing. grill-me interviews you until the plan has no holes left. diagnose runs a real debugging loop instead of guessing. handoff compresses the session so the next one doesn't start from zero. Three skills that fix the habits that waste your time.

3. https://t.co/csYwgltos5

Captures what the agent did, compresses it, and drops the useful part back into your next session. You stop re-explaining your own repo every single morning. The memory your coding agent should have shipped with.

4. https://t.co/v0s5pM9BHx

Type /graphify and it turns your whole codebase, docs, even screenshots, into a queryable map. Ask where auth lives and it walks the graph instead of cracking open files one at a time. The agent finally sees the shape of your project, not just the file in front of it.

5. https://t.co/lQOhG0FZWZ

A spec-driven workflow built for long tasks. When the context fills up, you pause, start fresh, and the plan is still exactly where you left it. This is how big builds stop quietly drifting off the rails three hours in.

6. https://t.co/MIdA6HGNOo

Makes the agent think like the laziest senior engineer in the room, the one who knows the best code is the code you never write. It's faster because it deletes scope, not because it types more. Scope creep, killed at the source.

7. https://t.co/BlxUEiyq6M

Cuts the fluff out of the agent's replies. Every token it wastes narrating what it's about to do is a token stolen from your actual code and error logs. Strips the chatter, hands the context window back to the work. Up to 65% fewer tokens.

8. https://t.co/lfzPJUQ4av

The harness around the model. Skills, memory, security checks, and research-first rules that run the same on Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor. One setup instead of four, so switching tools doesn't mean starting over.

9. https://t.co/nJpvRXloZ6

Splits the work into real roles, designer, engineering manager, QA, release. You stop asking one poor agent to design a thing, build it, and then review its own mess. A whole team out of one terminal, which is Garry Tan's actual setup.

10. https://t.co/YEMToFlmmH

One local gateway sitting in front of Claude Code and Codex. Point the cheap model at the easy edits and the strong model at the nasty bug, all without ever swapping tools. You stop overpaying for simple work and underpowering the hard stuff.

Most people run their coding agent straight out of the box.

The ones who install these are playing a completely different game.

text:
How do we shut down SF's drug market? Start with the data.

Five years ago, drug-dealing arrests hit a low: 1,780 a year.

Three years ago, the city launched the Drug Market Agency Coordination Center, uniting public health and public safety for the first time. Arrests spiked to 3,223 under then-Commander, now Chief, Lew. Convictions tripled from 16% to 46% under DA Jenkins.

It worked. The market shrank. Daytime dealing is gone.

So what's stopping us from finishing the job? Adaptation.

First, fewer dealers are left (good news!), with 1,948 arrested last year. But the ones who remain are harder to catch. They've switched from open dealing to drops and moved to nighttime, when police are stretched thin.

Second, judges keep letting them go. Of 1,172 pending dealing cases last year, only 10% were held pre-trial. Over 1,000 dealers went right back to the street.

To shut it down for good, we need to:

1. Put more police on the street at night
2. Launch a drug market intervention strategy that pairs prevention with enforcement
3. Hold judges accountable for releasing fentanyl dealers pre-trial
4. Change state law to treat fentanyl dealing as the deadly crime it is

text:
No official public ranking of SF judges by pretrial release rates exists, as the Superior Court does not release individual judge data. 

A 2023 Stop Crime SF study of 210 drug dealer detention motions (only 8 granted overall) ranked Judge Patrick Thompson highest by volume: 63 motions, 2 granted (~97% release). 

Limited other data notes Judge Michael Rhoads with 14 felony drug releases.

Is $swordcat merely a cat character that went viral because of its contrasting cuteness, or has it tapped into a cultural emotion capable of sustaining long-term attention?

5tCju6YNxHq5zrA6tGndr6F7TK42mpUFmeE31cSFpump 

I believe what is truly worth exploring is not simply the courage of the weak, but a more subtle contradiction within the character: the desire to become strong coexisting with an inability to escape the feeling of being weak. Compared with straightforward narratives of cuteness, combat, or underdog triumph, this contradiction is closer to the real psychological experiences of ordinary people and is more likely to resonate with them.

So, what exactly is Swordcat’s core narrative? I believe it is not simply a cute little cat holding an enormous sword, but the contrast of a seemingly weak character trying to play the role of someone strong. The cat itself remains soft, innocent, and even somewhat clumsy. Yet it puts on armor and raises a giant sword, as if it is already prepared to face whatever challenges lie ahead.

What makes this image interesting is that the cat has not actually become stronger. It has simply adopted the posture of someone strong. It is both imitating the powerful figure it aspires to become and using a somewhat comical display to conceal its inner insecurity.

This corresponds to a familiar experience in everyday life: even when we lack confidence, we still want to appear mature and strong enough to handle the problems in front of us. Perhaps Swordcat’s appeal lies in allowing people to laugh at their own helplessness while identifying with the part of themselves that refuses to give up.

If Swordcat is understood merely as a little cat holding a giant sword, its narrative is not particularly unique. The internet already has countless animal warriors, contrasting-cuteness characters, and underdog stories. What is truly worth paying attention to is why this character can simultaneously express the desire to “handle things in a mature way” and the desire to “become as fierce as those powerful figures.”

These two forms of expression may seem different, but they point to the same psychological impulse: people do not just want to have power. They also care about whether they look powerful.

Many people in real life do not actually have the ability to control every situation, yet they still have to take responsibility, face competition, and deal with all kinds of problems. As a result, maturity, composure, and toughness sometimes become social roles that people are required to play rather than reflections of their true emotional state.

Swordcat turns this psychology into an amusing image: a little cat that looks completely incapable of fighting, seriously holding a giant sword. It has neither the physique nor the aura of a powerful warrior, yet it is already fully equipped and standing in a posture that says it is ready for battle.

It is not telling people, “You can definitely become strong.” Instead, it portrays a more realistic state of mind: I may not be strong enough yet, but I want to be like someone who is.

What makes this emotion distinctive is that it combines admiration, self-mockery, anxiety, and a little defiance. It can be used to make fun of ourselves for pretending to be mature, but it can also express our longing for strength, independence, and control.

This gives Swordcat the potential to go beyond being a simple cute-animal Meme and become a character that expresses the psychological gap between how people feel and how they want to appear in real life.

Another strength lies in the visual design of the cat and the giant sword. This design effectively compresses multiple emotions into a single image.

Cats already have a broad emotional foundation in internet culture. They can be cute, lazy, arrogant, or innocent, and they can also be assigned all kinds of human personalities. When users see a cat, they usually do not need to understand any additional background to form an emotional connection.

However, a cat image on its own is unlikely to develop a distinctive narrative. Swordcat’s differentiation comes from the giant sword and knightly outfit.

A giant sword traditionally belongs to heroes, knights, and combat characters in video games. It usually symbolizes strength, authority, aggression, and challenge. When it appears in the paws of a tiny, innocent-looking cat, that traditionally serious heroic image becomes absurd.

More importantly, the giant sword is not just a funny prop. It gives the cat a character identity. It is no longer simply a cute animal being looked at. It becomes a character embarking on an adventure and preparing to face some kind of challenge.

This gives it room to tell stories continuously.

An ordinary cat can keep changing its expressions and backgrounds, but Swordcat can continually face new enemies, difficulties, and missions. It can represent an office worker dealing with work pressure, a little warrior facing a powerful opponent, or a clumsy hero trying to prove itself.

The cat provides emotional appeal, the giant sword creates character conflict, and the contrast between the two provides space for continuous creative expression.

This is also what distinguishes it from countless ordinary animal Memes. It does not rely solely on the humor of a single image. Instead, it has a character concept that users can easily expand upon.

From a token perspective, the early market logic behind swordcat first comes from an existing source of attention.

Many new Memes have to create a character, tell a story, and then wait for the market to accept them. Swordcat is different. The original cat video and its derivative expressions had already attracted attention on social platforms. When the token appeared, the market was not being introduced to a completely unfamiliar symbol.

For traders, this meant they could trade directly around an existing trend.

However, this alone is not enough to explain its valuation. What truly influences buying behavior is traders’ assessment of how much further this kind of viral attention could spread.

On the one hand, Swordcat has strong visual recognition. It is neither an ordinary cat nor a conventional powerful warrior. Instead, it combines two elements with a striking contrast. Such an image is easy to remember in a social media feed and easy for other users to recreate and share.

On the other hand, its expressive potential is not limited to a single emotion. It can be used for humor and self-mockery, but also to express the desire to become stronger, the refusal to give up, or the feeling of forcing oneself to face difficulties despite being unprepared. This means the same character can appear in different content contexts without relying entirely on repeated exposure to the original video.

For early Meme traders, these characteristics may indicate a longer attention lifecycle. What the market is buying is not just the attention that has already materialized, but also the potential for the character to attract additional attention in the future.

There is another factor that is easy to overlook: the token market trades expectations, not cultural value that has already been established.

When traders notice a character beginning to go viral, they may start positioning themselves in advance, betting that it will become the next popular Meme. As the price rises, trading volume increases, and social discussions spread, more traders may be drawn in, creating a short-term cycle between attention and liquidity.

As a result, the current market cap may simultaneously reflect the popularity of the original content, the character’s potential for further spread, market frontrunning sentiment, and liquidity expectations. It does not necessarily mean investors have already developed a deep cultural connection with Swordcat.

For swordcat, what really matters is whether it can turn one-time attention into sustained trading interest. If the original video continues to go viral but users have no interest in the token itself, the success of the Meme does not necessarily translate into the success of the token.

Finally, I believe there are several directions worth watching as Swordcat develops. These directions are not entirely separate from one another.

The first possibility is a shift from pretending to be strong to accepting one's own imperfections.

The current image has a strong sense of contrast. The little cat looks weak, yet it holds a giant sword, as if it is seriously playing a role it does not yet have the ability to fulfill.

If the community continues to use it to express everyday pressure, awkwardness, and self-mockery, Swordcat may gradually become a character representing the circumstances of ordinary people: people who lack the ability to solve every problem but still have to keep their lives going.

This form of communication does not require a grand story or a constant supply of new conflicts. Everyday life itself can provide an endless stream of material.

Its emotional meaning could gradually shift from simply “wanting to become stronger” to “I know I am imperfect, but I accept myself as I am.”

The advantage of this direction is that it offers a wide range of use cases and can easily generate ongoing everyday content. The risk, however, is that the emotion may become too diffuse, turning Swordcat into a generic cute reaction image and gradually eroding its distinctive identity.

The second possibility is a shift from imitating the strong to challenging them.

The giant sword and knightly appearance also give Swordcat the potential for a more intense narrative of confrontation.

At first, the cat simply wants to become like those powerful figures. But as the story develops, it may no longer be satisfied with imitation. It may begin challenging the very things that once made it feel weak.

This would bring a more obvious emotional shift: from admiration, imitation, and self-doubt toward resistance, defiance, and the desire to prove oneself.

This kind of content has considerable potential to spread within Meme culture because the contrast between strength and weakness is easy to understand and can easily be applied to real-world trends, gaming culture, and competition in the crypto market.

For example, when the market presents a clear contrast between strong and weak participants, Swordcat could be portrayed as the seemingly weak participant who refuses to surrender.

But this direction also has a problem. If Swordcat eventually becomes just another underdog hero, its original contrast may lose some of its appeal. Swordcat’s charm does not lie in eventually becoming an invincible warrior. It lies in the fact that it is not strong enough yet, but has already raised its giant sword with complete seriousness.

The third possibility is a shift from a simple character Meme toward a community culture built around shared identity.

This is the direction that could matter most to the token, but it is also the most difficult to achieve.

When a Meme character is repeatedly used by different users, what spreads may no longer be just images and captions. Instead, a shared identity may gradually form around it.

If Swordcat can continue attracting creators, the community may gradually give it a consistent personality, stories, and ways of behaving. Users would no longer simply borrow it to express a particular situation. They would begin identifying with the character itself.

At that point, Swordcat would no longer be just a cat image that can be casually replaced. It could develop its own cultural language.

However, community identification is not the same as token value. Even if Swordcat eventually becomes a widely used internet character, swordcat would still need to establish its own advantage in attracting attention among the many related tokens and content accounts.

Swordcat already has several characteristics worth paying attention to: a striking visual contrast, an easily understood emotional entry point, and room to expand from the original video into different everyday scenarios.

But these are only the starting conditions for cultural spread.

I believe the most important change to watch for is whether users begin actively assigning new meanings to Swordcat rather than simply repeating its original image.

If people continue using it to express the act of pretending to be mature, imitating the powerful, and forcing themselves to hold it together under pressure, Swordcat’s emotional identity may become increasingly recognizable.

If it starts developing its own stories, character relationships, and community-specific inside jokes, its spread may gradually shift from dependence on the original video to content actively produced by the community.

Conversely, if future content remains stuck at the visual contrast of a cat holding a giant sword, it may remain a short-lived viral image rather than a cultural symbol with lasting vitality.

From the token perspective, several other factors also need to be observed: whether discussions about Swordcat naturally lead to swordcat; whether the community remains consistently active; and whether changes in trading volume and holder numbers reflect genuine accumulation of attention rather than short-term, high-frequency turnover.

These factors are more useful for assessing its long-term potential than simple view counts or a single market-cap peak.

What is truly worth exploring about Swordcat is not the traditional underdog story of triumph over adversity. It is the contradiction between people's desire to embody strength and the ordinary nature they cannot escape in reality.

It has the urge to imitate the powerful, but also the helplessness of facing reality. It wants to appear mature and tough, yet still retains a clumsy, cute, and bewildered side.

This is an extremely common psychological state in everyday life, yet few characters can express it so directly.

A little cat stands on the battlefield, seriously holding a giant sword. It may have no idea whether it can win, but at least in that moment, it looks ready.

What swordcat is betting on is whether this visually distinctive cat character can evolve from a viral video into a cultural symbol that embodies the psychological contradiction of “wanting to become strong while still being an ordinary person,” and ultimately become the market’s primary token expression of that symbol.

Its opportunity lies in the universality of its emotional entry point, the distinctiveness of its visual identity, and the potential for its content to expand continuously. Its risk is that these advantages currently exist more as potential for wider reach than as an established community culture or value exclusive to the token.

If Swordcat can eventually evolve from “an amusing little cat knight” into a character that users repeatedly return to and continually give new stories to, its narrative may genuinely move beyond a one-time viral trend. Otherwise, even if it reaches its current market cap, it may simply remain a short-term Meme trade driven jointly by external traffic and market expectations.

$APT 38 ms → at commit

$SUI 69 ms → at commit
$SOMI 100 ms → at commit
$SOL 269 ms → ~12.8 s
$TON 414 ms → ~0.8 s
$CRO 429 ms → at commit
$BNB 450 ms → ~0.65 s
$SEI 472 ms → at commit
$ICP 480 ms → at commit
$NEAR 589 ms → ~1.2 s
$EGLD 600 ms → ~100–250 ms intra-shard, ~2.4 s cross-shard
$KTA 686 ms → at commit
$KAIA 1 s → ~1 s

$FOGO is #2 on blocks, not on finality. $SOL produces a block in 269 ms and finalizes in ~12.8 s. $EGLD is #12 on cadence, not on irreversibility.
